newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia 10-yr bond futures wipe out 1994 memory.
newsitem.headline: Australia 10-yr bond futures wipe out 1994 memory.

text.p: The Australian 10-year bond futures contract set a new all time high of 93.640 on Thursday, overtaking the previous peak of 93.630 set in early 1994, as the market geared itself up for another easing in monetary policy.

The contract, which was listed on the Sydney Futures Exchange in December 1984, has now retraced the massive sell-off in 1994 when global debt markets went into meltdown after the U.S. Federal Reserve went into an agressive tightening cycle.

That sell-off took the contract to 89.140 by November 1994, or a rise of some 450 basis points in bond yields within a year. Today's move followed weaker than expected second quarter wages data which fuelled already strong expectations of a 50 basis point easing by the Reserve Bank in the official 5.5 percent interest rate as early as Friday.
"The 10-year bond yields have a hit a new post-deregulation low of under 6.4 percent in the wake of the wages data," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
"While there remains the risk the market will overshoot these levels a little more ... it might be a case to sell the fact once the interest rate cut announcement is made," he added.
However, there are reasons to believe that that the market is on a firming footing this time round than when it caved in to a tumbling U.S. Treasury market in 1994.
"For one, you are looking at a relatively better inflation position than it was going back to 1993," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.

Second quarter inflation reported on Wednesday showed the underlying rate at 1.7 percent, its lowest level since the series began in 1971. Today's wages data, which showed the annual rate running at its lowest since August 1994 at 3.7 percent, confirmed that inflation may stay low for some time.
Also, back in late 1993 the Federal Reserve gave very stern warnings on what it intended to do on policy to curb inflation which led to a series of interest rate increases in 1994.
"So the smoking gun of the Fed was always overhanging the market," Roberts said.

However, so far this cycle, the Fed has tightened policy just once in March, and following this week's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, Fed chairman Alan Greenspan appears to be in no desperate hurry to hike again.
Greenspan said on Tuesday that U.S. growth was slowing, heading off the need to raise interest rates for now, and was also confident that U.S. inflation would be modest in 1997.

Roberts also noted that by this stage of the cycle last time round institutions were heavily invested in the rally, but this this time they appear to be comparatively cautious running through this late stage of the rally.
"So you haven't got the excessive overleveraged positions at this point as you did last time, so cautiously that means that this rally can progress a bit further," Roberts added.
